**WHEN A RECIPE IS LINKED TO AN EXISTING MATERIAL, THE MATERIAL'S PURCHASE
PRICE WINS. THE RECIPE'S OWN COST DOES NOT OVERWRITE IT.** §29's core text
says a linked material's *"cost is derived from its recipe rather than from a
purchase price."* That is still true of a recipe materialized as a BRAND NEW
material — `materializeNew()`, no purchase history, nothing to defer to — and
**it stops being true the moment that recipe is instead linked to a material
that already had one** — `materializeLink()`, an existing `ingredients` row
with its own `buy_price`. This addendum narrows the original sentence rather
than reversing it: read it as true only where the material has no purchase
price of its own.

**Rationale.** The material was bought, and that is what it cost. Where a
recipe and a bought material are the same physical thing, the recipe
describes what was done to it — repacked, portioned, relabelled — not where
it came from. Costing that event from the recipe instead of the purchase
would price a bag of bought powder by what the kitchen scale says it weighs
rather than by what the supplier invoiced, and the two have no reason to
agree.

**The live example is not hypothetical — it is the 12-of-16 pattern a
same-day audit surfaced.** Running the exact `ensureMaterialized()` check
read-only across all 137 recipes found 16 that would collide with an
existing, unlinked `ingredients` row — 11 of them one shape repeated: a
recipe named identically to a bought raw material (Organic Kale Powder,
Organic Matcha Powder, Organic Moringa Powder, Organic Chlorella Powder,
Organic Turmeric Powder, Organic Spirulina Powder, Organic Garlic Powder,
Organic Onion Powder, Sumac, Extra Virgin Coconut Oil, Coconut Flakes), plus
BioCurcumin+ (Organic) colliding on SKU rather than name. A bulk powder
bought from a supplier, repacked into a jar via a recipe, is exactly this
addendum's case: once a human links one of those 12 recipes to its bought
material via `materializeLink()`, the rollup must not then quietly replace
the supplier's price with the recipe's.

**Not decided here: the detection mechanism.** Whether this is read from
`buy_price > 0` at write time, from whether the link was made via
`materializeLink` versus `materializeNew`, or some other signal, is left to
whichever PR touches `lib/recipe-rollup.js`'s write path — deferred
deliberately, the same way §29's first addendum deferred its own mechanism,
because naming one here would bind an implementation this document doesn't
own. **The 16 collisions themselves are not resolved by this addendum and
are not being resolved in code** — Ash clears them by hand; this only
settles what must happen to cost once one of them IS linked.

Evidence: the 16-collision audit run against `/root/roots-v2/data/roots.db`
on 2026-08-27, read-only, no rows written.

## 30. Channel sync — what must stay true

Seven rules governing any sync between Tacet and an external system a business sells through. They are stated as intent and name no table, column, constant or function on purpose: the implementations they were learned from will be replaced, and a rule that names one outlives the reason it named it. The evidence is in `docs/eleme-findings.md`, opened 2026-08-25 and extended since; if that document and these rules disagree, the rules stand and the evidence is stale.

1. A CHANGE IS NOT SYNCED UNTIL THE CHANNEL CONFIRMS IT. Our record of what we sent is evidence of our intent, never evidence of the channel's state. Where a channel can be read back, the read-back is the only proof of success.

2. EVERY CHANNEL MUST HAVE A RECOVERY PATH THAT CAN REACH A TARGET FROM ANY STATE IT CAN ENTER, INCLUDING TOTAL FAILURE. No failure may be terminal.

3. A VALUE THAT BINDS OUR RECORD TO AN EXTERNAL SYSTEM MUST BE SELECTED FROM VALUES THAT SYSTEM SUPPLIED. Never typed by a person, never composed by us. THIS IS THE SAME PRINCIPLE AS THE LOCKED-VOCABULARY RULE: `docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md` Rules 4 — *"CN strings are locked here. Never compose new Chinese; copy from these tables"* — applies it to language, and this rule applies it to identity. Copy from the source, never compose. A reader meeting either should read them as one constraint on two surfaces, not two.

4. WHERE THE CORRECT TARGET OR QUANTITY CANNOT BE DETERMINED, THE SYSTEM REFUSES AND SURFACES THE PROBLEM. It never substitutes a placeholder. A visible failure is always preferable to a fabricated value reaching a customer.

5. AN ALARM MUST BE CLEARABLE BY THE MECHANISM THAT RAISED IT. An alarm that only a human with database access can clear will be ignored, and then so will the ones that matter.

6. A PENDING CHANGE WHOSE DESIRED END STATE IS ALREADY TRUE IS COMPLETE, WHATEVER ITS RECORDED STATUS.

7. WHERE A TARGET IS CHOSEN BY MATCHING, THE CHOICE IS RECORDED, NOT ONLY THE OUTCOME. A system that resolves among candidates stores which one it picked, alongside what it sent and when. Storing only that a change succeeded makes every later question an argument from inference: the record can say a quantity went out and cannot say where it landed. That is worse than a wrong match, because a wrong match with the choice written down is a question anyone can answer afterwards, and a wrong match without it is not answerable at all — the fault becomes unresolvable rather than merely undetected. This is not an argument against matching, and it does not soften rule 4: where the right target cannot be determined the system still refuses. It governs the case where a target WAS determined, and says the determination is part of what happened. Exposure is not uniform — the more a channel leans on names rather than on a stable value that system supplied, the more often the choice is the only interesting part of the record — and the ordering across our channels, with the code behind it, is in the worked example. That example is finding 9 in `docs/eleme-findings.md`: one push of a real quantity resolved to one of three possible listings, and which one is still not established.

**THE CHANNEL ORDERING RULE 7 POINTS AT, AND WHAT IT ORDERS BY.** Rewritten 2026-08-26 (v4.81); the correction that produced it is marked below. Rule 7 itself is untouched — this is the supporting statement it defers to, not the rule.

**The ordering is: Meituan worst, then Eleme, then 闪购, then GZ Grocery.**

**It orders by STANDING EXPOSURE — how many of our mappings are one external edit away from a silent wrong write, and whether anything downstream would catch one if it happened.** It does NOT order by how badly a matching rule could misbehave in the abstract. The basis is written down because the two bases give different answers, and the earlier line said "ordering of exposure" and left the word to the reader.

- **Meituan — worst.** The containment test compares a candidate against our name truncated to its leading same-script run, so **133 of 393 named mappings resolve onto a neighbour** the moment their own listing is renamed or delisted. Nothing downstream catches it: the drift sweep compares our record of what we sent against our own shelf count and never reads the channel's stock, and no push record says which listing answered.
- **Eleme — second.** Still name-only and still with no article number, so the name remains the only key. But it now refuses an inexact name rather than taking one, and it records the listing each push landed on, so a mislanding would be answerable afterwards. Seven mappings sit one rename away from a neighbour whose name contains theirs.
- **闪购 — mild.** Our own article number is looked up first and the name is consulted only when that misses.
- **GZ Grocery — none.** No name matching in the push path at all; it targets a stored stable id the channel supplied.

**THE TWO AT THE TOP ARE UNLIKE EACH OTHER, AND THE DIFFERENCE MATTERS MORE THAN THE ORDER.** Without it the order gets misread as "Meituan has been going wrong and Eleme has not", which is the opposite of what happened. **Meituan's exposure is LATENT** — zero mappings use the loose branch today, every one that resolves resolves exactly, and it fires only on a merchant-side rename or delist, at which point 133 of 393 land on a neighbour. **Eleme's was LIVE** — a fragment resolved and wrote, at least once, and which of three listings took the quantity is still not established. **And Meituan's damage is worse when it fires**, because the truncation collapses families of SIZE VARIANTS onto one key: a mis-resolve swaps two live stock numbers, the sibling that took the push and our own product which believes it pushed, rather than writing an obviously wrong number onto an unrelated stranger somebody notices. **Eleme has already done harm and can no longer do it that way; Meituan has not yet done harm and would do more of it.** Both are true, of different questions, and the ordering answers the first.

> **CORRECTION, 2026-08-26 — the ordering was rewritten. Marked, not silently replaced.**
>
> **It previously read:** *"Eleme worst, matching a substring in either direction … then Meituan, substring but one direction only, tempered by an exact-match-first preference and a shortest-name tiebreak."* That shipped in v4.79 and was left standing through v4.80 while the question was put to Ash. He ruled; this is the rewrite.
>
> **What was understated.** *"Substring but one direction only, tempered by …"* is accurate about the arm it names and the damage is not in that arm. The containment test's middle arm compares the candidate against our name **truncated to its leading same-script run**, so a family of size variants all reduce to the same key: of the 133 exposed mappings, **1 is exposed through the whole-name arm that was described and 132 through the truncation that was not.** The shortest-name tiebreak, offered as tempering, was written to prefer a base product over a combo sharing its prefix; among four pack sizes it picks whichever the merchant named most tersely, which makes the choice deterministic rather than right.
>
> **What moved the order, and neither is a change of opinion.** Eleme's both-directions branch no longer exists, so the fact that put Eleme first is a property of deleted code; and Meituan is worse on both counts — 133 exposed mappings against Eleme's seven, and nothing downstream that would catch a mislanding, where Eleme now records the target.
>
> **The basis is now stated in the text**, which is the third change and the one that stops this recurring: on one honest reading of the old word "exposure", Eleme still ranks first, and naming the basis settles which question is being answered instead of leaving two answers to compete.
>
> The identical rewrite and the identical mark are in `docs/eleme-findings.md` finding 9, which carries this ordering as its own, done in the same pass so the two cannot drift apart. Evidence: `docs/meituan-findings.md` findings 1, 4, 5 and 9.

**Amendment (2 Sep 2026): when no locked source exists.**

The rule stands: Chinese strings are copied from locked sources, never
composed. But a locked source does not always exist, and the rule previously
gave no route forward — work stalled rather than proceeding.

When a new string has no locked source, in order of preference:

1. **Lift from the channel.** If the string names something a platform
   already displays to us — a fee, a status, a settlement line — use the
   platform's own wording verbatim. Meituan's and Eleme's merchant screens
   are locked sources for their own vocabulary. Record which platform and
   which screen.

2. **Ask the operator.** For anything staff-facing with no channel
   equivalent, Ash asks whoever runs the store. Their wording beats a
   correct translation.

3. **Compose provisionally, and mark it.** Only when 1 and 2 are unavailable
   or would block delivery. The string ships marked PROVISIONAL in
   docs/tacet-delivery-vocabulary.md and is reviewed by a native operator
   before the feature leaves beta. Composing is a last resort with a debt
   attached, not a shortcut.

Never invent silently. A composed string that is not marked provisional is
a rule violation regardless of whether it turns out to be correct.

## 31. Product unit cost — contents plus packaging

Nine rules governing what a product costs and where its packaging attaches. Like §30's they are stated as intent and name no table, column, screen or function, and for the same reason: this settles what is TRUE, and the schema, the screens and the migration are later work that must answer to these rules rather than the rules being written around whatever gets built. The evidence is `docs/packaging-findings.md`, findings 2, 3, 4, 6, 9 and 12; if that document and these rules disagree, the rules stand and the evidence is stale.

**Why this is its own section and not a §29 addendum.** §29 is about the recipe graph — a made thing is a material, a recipe line points at exactly one target, and its second addendum settles which of a recipe's costs travel along that line when one recipe feeds another. This settles what a PRODUCT costs. The two touch at exactly one point, rule 5 below, and everything else here is on the other side of a boundary §29 draws itself when it closes with *"Recipes are not connected to retail Products in this phase."* More to the point, rule 7 is the governing constraint of this section and it says the packaging half must work with no recipe anywhere in the picture: filing that inside the section about recipes would put a rule whose entire purpose is independence from recipes underneath the heading that assumes them, where a reader looking for how a tenant with no kitchen prices a bag of almonds would never think to look.

1. **A PRODUCT'S UNIT COST IS ITS CONTENTS PLUS ITS PACKAGING.** Contents come from a recipe, from a purchase price, or from a figure entered directly — whichever of the three the tenant has. **NEITHER HALF IS MANDATORY.** A product may have contents and no packaging, packaging and no contents, or neither, and each of those is a real business rather than an incomplete record.

2. **PACKAGING IS CHOSEN ON THE PRODUCT, NOT ON THE RECIPE.** One recipe backs several products that are packed differently, and the recipe cannot know which of them is being priced. **Crunchy Granola is the worked example**: one recipe, a ¥43 jar and an ¥8 sample pack. The sample pack is the same food in a smaller container, and today it is DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED from recipe-linking, because linking it would hand it the jar's packaging and the model has nowhere else to put its own — a product held out of its own recipe to stop the recipe costing it wrongly. **Hummus Asli was cited here as the same shape at scale, and it is not this rule's case at all.** Two recipes carry that name — 7 (SKU 1-12) and 92 (SKU 1-10) — sharing both `name_en` and `name_cn`, so the two-of-three matching at `database.js:4263` cannot resolve either, both are skipped as ambiguous at `:4332`, and the products hold **no recipe link at all**. That makes them rules 7 and 8's case — packaging with no recipe anywhere in the picture — rather than this rule's. **Crunchy Granola above is this rule's only worked example.** Recorded as `docs/packaging-findings.md` finding 18.

   *Recorded so it is not restored later as something mislaid: the "six products at four price points" and the "single 300ml box" that stood in this rule through v4.92 were REMOVED as UNSOURCED, not lost — neither had a query behind it, and the 300ml box was recipe 9's (`docs/packaging-findings.md:314-315`).*

3. **A PRODUCT CARRIES A LIST OF PACKAGING MATERIALS, NOT ONE.** Roots packs a jar, a sticker and a label — three materials on one product. The model records one, so two of the three are **not costed at all**. **THIS IS NOT A VARIANT PROBLEM AND IT IS NOT A FUTURE ONE**: it is wrong on ordinary flat products today, on the plainest case the system has, and it means the packaging cost this business reports is understated by whatever the sticker and the label come to.

4. **PACKAGING IS A MATERIAL LIKE ANY OTHER.** It is already bought from a supplier, priced on a purchase order and recorded as a material. A second, standalone list of packaging duplicates the same physical object with a price typed by hand, and the two copies have **already drifted from what was paid** — which is what a duplicate always does eventually, and here it has done it already, so this is an observation rather than a prediction. **ONE RECORD PER PHYSICAL THING.**

5. **THE RECIPE CARRIES NO PACKAGING.** A recipe is what it costs to MAKE the food, and nothing else. That is also exactly the figure a sub-recipe needs when its output feeds another recipe, so this rule is not a second decision: it makes visible in the screens the separation that `c86ef74e` already made in the numbers under §29's second addendum. One statement of where packaging belongs, holding in the arithmetic and on the page.

6. **PACKAGING DOES NOT DEPLETE STOCK.** Ash's decision. Buying five hundred jars and using five hundred jars leave the same record; packaging is a cost, not an inventory. **No material depletes anything today**, so this holds with no work at all — and it is written down as a DECISION for precisely that reason. Left unrecorded it looks like an omission, and an omission invites a later reader to fix it.

7. **NOTHING IN THE PACKAGING HALF MAY ASSUME A KITCHEN.** No servings, no batch sizes, no yield, no unit that only means something to someone who cooks. **THIS IS THE GOVERNING CONSTRAINT AND IT OUTRANKS THE OTHERS.** §0 requires that any business in any country be able to use Tacet, and a shop bagging almonds it bought from a supplier, or a butcher wrapping a tray, has packaging and no kitchen whatever. A model that can only be reached through a recipe does not merely inconvenience those tenants — **it locks them out entirely**, and it does so silently, because the screen that would price their packaging is one they are never shown.

8. **A PRODUCT WITH NO RECIPE CAN STILL HAVE PACKAGING.** The reseller case, stated separately from rule 7 because it is the concrete instance that proves the constraint is reachable rather than aspirational: a bought-in product, boxed and sold, is a complete and correct record under these rules with no recipe ever created. That is why the design generalises instead of being a kitchen model with an exception bolted to it.

9. **AN EMPTY PACKAGING LIST MEANS UNKNOWN, NOT ZERO.** Ash's decision. A missing packaging figure is a hard zero today, which is why a product nobody has filled in is **indistinguishable** from one that genuinely has no packaging — and why it reports a margin that is too good, in the direction that flatters. Unknown keeps the one-time migration pass visible while it is incomplete, instead of a half-done pass looking finished. **AND THERE MUST BE AN EXPLICIT WAY TO SAY "NO PACKAGING"**, so the reseller selling loose goods is CORRECT rather than merely unfinished. Unknown and zero are two different facts and the system must be able to hold both.

**Consequences, not decisions.** Three things follow from the rules above. They are recorded so none of them is met later as a surprise, and none of them is a choice being made here.

- **Costs will RISE wherever packaging was under-counted**, because three components are counted where one was. **This is the opposite direction from `c86ef74e`, which lowered costs by removing a packaging share nobody bought, and it has exactly the same purpose.** Both make the number honest. Neither is aiming at a number, and a reader who sees only the direction of travel will read one of them as contradicting the other.

- **65 products carry a packaging figure through their recipe today, and each one needs its packaging picked once.** That one-time pass is **the real cost of this change** — not the code. Any plan that budgets the build and not the pass has budgeted the cheap half.

- **A gift box holding several different products is not covered by this.** It is a finished good with no recipe of its own that references other PRODUCTS rather than materials — a third shape, and not the one settled here. **RECORDED AS A KNOWN LIMIT OF THIS DESIGN, NOT AS SOMETHING TO SOLVE NOW.**

**What the rules rest on, in the code as it stands.** Named here rather than inside the rules, so the rules outlive the implementation they were learned from:

- Packaging lives on the recipe and there is **no packaging column on a product at all**, so "what does packaging cost for this product" is not a question the product can answer — finding 2.
- The sample pack's exclusion from recipe auto-linking is `isScaledPack()` at `database.js:4293` — rule 2's worked example, in one predicate.
- A missing packaging figure reads as zero at `lib/recipe-cost.js:150` — rule 9's fault, in one line. The module already returns a flag that would tell the two apart, and no screen branches on it — finding 6.
- The standalone `packaging_types` table: 44 rows created in one sitting, no foreign key and no link to materials of any kind, **8 of 21 name-matched pairs already disagreeing** with what purchasing paid, and no update logged anywhere — findings 3, 4 and 12. The same physical jar is priced in four independent places and nothing compares any two of them.
- **Nothing depletes any material** — not packaging, not flour — because there is no stock column on materials and no material-stock table. Rule 6 costs nothing to hold today for that reason — finding 9.

**Deliberately not settled here: the schema, the screens and the migration.** This section settles what is true. How it is built comes later, and must answer to these rules.

### §31 addendum — a build line is the product's only cost source (decided 2026-08-27)

**A PRODUCT HAS EXACTLY ONE COST SOURCE, AND `recipe_id` IS NOT A SECOND ONE.**
Once a product carries a build list, nothing may read its `recipe_id` to derive
`unit_cost` — the build list is authoritative, full stop. This settles the
question rule 1 left open about HOW "contents come from a recipe" reaches the
product: it does not reach it directly. A recipe's output is a MATERIAL per §29,
so a product whose content is cooked gets there the same way any bought-in
product does — a build line pointing at that material, quantified the same way a
box or a label is. **Rule 1 is not reversed by this** — a product's cost is
still contents plus packaging, and contents can still ultimately be
recipe-derived — but it is made mechanically exact: there is one mechanism, a
build line, and a recipe's cost reaches a product only by first becoming a
material's cost, never as a parallel read of `store_products.recipe_id`.

**The reason is the reason §29 gave for the same shape.** A recipe line pointing
at either a material or a recipe was rejected because every reader would need to
handle two cases — the same branching-implementations pattern that produced five
divergent copies of the recipe cost formula. A product cost sourced from either a
build list or a linked recipe is the identical shape one level up, and it is
rejected for the identical reason: one mechanism, one target, no reader ever
asked to handle a second case that might disagree with the first.

**`recipe_id` survives, narrowed to the one job this does not touch.**
`routes/products.js`'s allergen rollup reads a product's linked recipe for its
ingredients' allergen lists — a different question from what something costs,
unaffected by this addendum, and the column is not removed.

Evidence and the mechanism this settles ahead of building:
`docs/tacet-product-build-lines-design.md` §7, written against
`docs/packaging-findings.md` Appendix B.

## 32. Waste is a stock movement with a reason

Thirteen decisions settling what waste IS, what is built and what is deliberately not. Like §30's and §31's they are stated as intent and name no table, column, screen or function, and for the same reason: this settles what is true, and the schema, the screens and the migration are later work that must answer to these rules rather than the rules being written around whatever gets built. The evidence is `docs/tacet-waste-survey.md`, the read-only survey of 2026-08-26; if that document and these rules disagree, the rules stand and the evidence is stale.

1. **WASTE IS NOT A FEATURE, IT IS A REASON.** Stock going down for any cause that is not a sale is ONE mechanism, and waste is one of the reasons that mechanism records. It is not a parallel system with its own arithmetic. **The kitchen app's waste screen is a log that moves no stock, and that is a defect rather than a model to port** — a business can record fifty units lost and still be offering all fifty for sale on every channel.

2. **THE KITCHEN WASTE SCREEN IS NOT MIGRATED. IT IS REPLACED.** `waste_entries` is not back-migrated and the three live rows are abandoned. The kitchen screen stays live until Roots is cut over, then is retired. **This deliberately abandons history, and the reason is recorded so it is not later met as an oversight:** the table holds three rows, and its `product_id` points at the KITCHEN products table rather than at the store catalogue — the id-space hazard the survey records as H1, where the two tables share ids only for rows that existed at fork time and have had independent keys ever since. Building fresh against `store_products` removes that hazard; back-migrating three rows would carry it in.

3. **ONE MECHANISM, TWO SUBJECTS.** A waste record's subject is either a MATERIAL or a PRODUCT. **It is a field, not a fork, and two features must never be built here.** A product subject resolves against the store catalogue; a material subject resolves against the materials master. Exactly one of the two is set on any row. §21 keeps Products and Materials as separate modules and this does not soften that — the two lists stay two lists; what is shared is the movement, not the master.

4. **THE MATERIAL SUBJECT REQUIRES THE PRODUCTION MODULE; THE PRODUCT SUBJECT DOES NOT.** A pure retail account that makes nothing still wastes finished stock — a dropped jar, a case damaged in transit, a short-dated line pulled off the shelf. **Waste therefore carries its own account-level toggle and is not gated behind Production.** Enabling Production adds the material subject to a mechanism that was already there; it does not switch waste on.

5. **RECIPES ARE NOT A DEPENDENCY.** A product's cost is the stored scalar on the product. A material's cost is its own stored cost. Neither needs a recipe. **This closes the dependency the survey raised against §28's Phase 1 boundary** — the kitchen implementation values a wasted product through its recipe and falls back to the SELL PRICE when it cannot, which books a loss at retail and requires the Recipes work §28 defers. Costing from the stored figure needs nothing deferred, and it is what §31 already establishes a product's unit cost to be.

6. **RECORDING WASTE MOVES STOCK.** It writes a stock ledger row and the on-hand number goes down. **A loss that leaves the number unchanged records nothing** — it forces a second manual adjustment somewhere else, which will sometimes not happen, and the gap between the two is invisible until a count. The stock ledger already reserves `waste` as a reason value and nothing writes it today, which is the shape of the defect in one line: the model was anticipated and never connected.

7. **REASON CODES ARE MANDATORY.** A quantity with no reason cannot answer the only question worth asking, which is whether less should have been made. **The seeded set is fixed in this phase and is not account-editable:** spoiled, expired, damaged, preparation error, staff consumption, sampling, other. **`Other` requires a note.**

8. **A DISCOUNTED SALE IS NOT WASTE.** Unsold stock sold cheap at close is REVENUE and belongs in Orders. It must never be recordable as waste, in either direction: a sale is not a loss, and recording it as one both understates takings and overstates spoilage, so the two errors hide each other. **Stock taken by staff is a real cost but a different one**, and it gets its own reason code rather than being folded into spoilage — a business that gives food to its team is not a business throwing food away, and a number that merges them cannot be acted on.

9. **COST IS SNAPSHOT AT ENTRY, NEVER RECOMPUTED.** A later price change must not restate a past loss. What a thing cost on the day it was lost is what it cost.

10. **NO COST AVAILABLE IS NOT ZERO COST.** The row saves, cost is stored as absent, and the row is flagged UNCOSTED. **Reports show the count of uncosted rows alongside the total** rather than silently understating the loss. Storing zero — which is today's behaviour, and which saves without warning — is a defect: a loss nobody could price and a loss that genuinely cost nothing render identically, and the total reads as complete when it is not. This is the same distinction §31 rule 9 draws between unknown and zero, applied to a movement rather than to a master record.

11. **ENTRIES ARE NEVER EDITED OR DELETED.** A mistake is VOIDED, which writes a reversal row and returns the stock. This follows §20 and needs no separate justification here; it is stated because the kitchen implementation hard-deletes, keeping no record of what the deleted row said.

12. **DATES RESOLVE IN THE ACCOUNT'S TIME ZONE.** The survey found every date on the waste path is UTC while the business runs at UTC+8, so a loss recorded before eight in the morning lands on the previous day. **The business date a waste row belongs to is resolved against the account's configured time zone, not the server's.** Subject to §0: the zone is an account setting, not a constant.

13. **A CLOSE ROUTINE IS A SEPARATE, LATER PIECE OF WORK.** An end-of-day sweep listing a location's perishable products, so a person confirms what is left rather than remembering what was lost, is how the number becomes RELIABLE rather than merely available. But it is a screen writing these same rows, and it needs a perishable flag on products that does not exist. **It is deliberately not in this phase, and building this phase must not make it harder** — the rows it would write are the rows defined here, and nothing in this phase may assume every waste row was typed one at a time.

**Open, not decided here.** Recorded as deferred rather than settled, so none of them is later treated as closed by silence:

- **Whether reason codes become account-editable.** Rule 7 fixes the set for this phase only. Whether an account may add, rename or retire a code — and what that does to reporting across a change — is not decided.
- **Whether waste feeds a production or purchasing signal.** Repeated spoilage on one line is evidence that too much is being made or too much is being bought, and nothing here decides whether waste data reaches either module or stays a report.
- **The perishable flag.** Rule 13 names it as the close routine's prerequisite and does not design it: what carries it, whether it is a flag or a shelf life, and whether it belongs to the product or to the product at a location are all open.

### §32 addendum — the material subject is deferred, the date anchors on the location, and cost stores a resolved total (decided 2026-08-27)

Three decisions made when the first build against §32 was scoped, and made because that build stopped before anything was written rather than choosing its way past them. **Rules 3, 6 and 12 are NOT rewritten and nothing above is edited away** — point 2 changes what rule 12 resolves against and says so; points 1 and 3 answer questions §32 left to the build. A fourth item is recorded as open and is deliberately not resolved here.

1. **THE MATERIAL SUBJECT IS DEFERRED, NOT DROPPED.** Materials have no stock and no ledger today — there is no stock column on the materials master and no material stock table — and **§31 rule 6 records that as a decision rather than a gap**, which is why it cannot be treated as an oversight to patch around. **Rules 3 and 6 therefore cannot both hold for a material subject**: rule 3 requires the subject to be either a material or a product, and rule 6 requires recording waste to move stock, which for a material there is no stock to move. **The resolution is that the record's SHAPE is unchanged** — subject type, both nullable keys, exactly one of them set — **and the material subject is refused at the API until material stock exists.** Rule 3's purpose was to prevent two features being built here, and **that purpose is served by the shape, not by shipping both subjects together**: one table, one constraint, one code path, with one of its two subjects not yet accepted. **Rule 6 holds unbroken**, because nothing that has no stock can be recorded at all. **Material waste unblocks when material stock is designed, which is its own decision and must not be smuggled into a waste build.**

2. **THE BUSINESS DATE RESOLVES FROM THE LOCATION, NOT THE ACCOUNT.** Rule 12 says the account's time zone. **There is no account time zone in the schema; there is a per-location one.** And the location is the better anchor regardless of what exists — **waste always occurs somewhere**, so the place it happened is a fact about the event rather than a setting standing in for one, and an account spanning two zones would otherwise date a loss by neither of them. **Rule 12 is amended to read: the business date a waste row belongs to is resolved in the time zone of the LOCATION the waste occurred at, falling back to the system default where a location has none.** The rest of rule 12 stands unchanged, including its subjection to §0 — the zone is configured, never a constant.

3. **COST IS STORED AS A RESOLVED TOTAL IN WHOLE CENTS.** Computed once at entry as unit cost times quantity and rounded there. **§24's exclusion of whole cents for per-unit costs applies to RATES that get multiplied downstream** — a per-gram figure rounded to a cent and then multiplied by a thousand carries the rounding error a thousand times, which is the defect that decision exists to prevent. **This is the product of that multiplication, already resolved, and nothing downstream multiplies it again.** The unit cost is read in whatever the live convention holds it in and converted at the boundary. This does not reopen §24 and does not generalise beyond this column.

**Open, and NOT resolved here: §24's money rule names an arbiter that no longer exists.** §24's rule MONEY IS RESOLVED BY SCHEMA CLASS, NEVER BY COLUMN NAME defines a money column as one that `scripts/postgres-full-copy/plan.json` gives conversion class CENTS or NUM6, and states that **no other test is permitted**. That file was deleted with the cancelled Postgres migration. **The rule as written therefore cannot be applied by anyone**, in either direction: there is no permitted way to establish that a column is money, and none to establish that it is not. Point 3 above settles one column on its own reasoning and deliberately does not stand in for the general answer. **This needs its own decision pass** — it is wider than waste, it reaches every future money column, and it is recorded here only because this build was the first thing to walk into it.

## 33. Whether a wasted item's packaging is lost is an account policy

**Decision.** Whether the packaging of a wasted item counts as part of the loss is an ACCOUNT POLICY, not a platform rule, and neither answer may be hardcoded. Every route that costs waste reads one shared account-level setting; none of them decides for itself.

**Why it cannot be a platform rule.** The honest answer differs by business and both businesses are real. A shop that packs at the point of sale and bins the container along with the product has genuinely lost that packaging — the jar goes in the bin with what was in it. A kitchen that discards unpacked prep has lost none, because nothing was ever packed. Hardcoding either answer is not a simplification; it is a decision to be wrong for one of those businesses, and §0 does not permit that.

**Roots' answer is that the container IS lost.** Roots packs before the shelf, so a wasted unit takes its jar, its sticker and its label with it. **THAT IS ROOTS' SETTING, NOT THE PLATFORM DEFAULT**, and it must not reach the code as a constant. A future account that answers the other way must be able to do so by configuration, not by a patch.

**This is adjacent to §29's rule and is NOT an amendment to it.** §29's second addendum settles that A COST DERIVED FROM MAKING A THING IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A COST OF USING IT — packaging belongs to the serving that is SOLD and does not travel to a parent recipe CONSUMING the material. That rule governs two ways a thing leaves: sold, or consumed. **Destroyed is a third case, and neither of the first two answers it.** A container that does not travel to a consumer may still be lost when the unit it holds is binned, and §29's reasoning — that the bulk half goes into reused kitchen tubs nobody costs — says nothing about a sellable unit that is thrown away in its packaging. Reading §33 as a restatement of §29 gets both wrong.

### 🔴 LIVE DEFECT — the policy is hardcoded in two places with opposite values, and both are in production

**Not yet fixed, and stated as a defect rather than a design.** Two waste routes are mounted in the same process and disagree about this question, so **the same wasted item costs a different amount depending on which route recorded it.**

- **The kitchen route EXCLUDES the parent recipe's packaging** (`routes/waste.js:56`), rebuilding a packaging-free batch total. Its reasoning is written into the file: a container is recycled onto the replacement unit, so counting it would double-count.
- **The retail route INCLUDES it.** It reads `store_products.unit_cost` (`lib/product-cost.js`), which the cascade writes as `costPerServing` — and that figure contains `packagingTotal`.

**Under Roots' policy the retail route is correct and the kitchen route understates a loss.** But **the divergence is wrong under either policy**, because one of the two is always wrong and nothing reconciles them.

**IT WAS NEVER A DECISION.** Nothing in the retail route argues that a wasted product incurs its packaging; nothing in it acknowledges the kitchen route's recycled-container reasoning. It arrived as a consequence of reading a stored column — which is what §32 rule 5 asks for, and what §31 rule 1 establishes that column to contain. Both rules were followed and the question was never put. **This is recorded so that fixing it is understood as settling a question nobody asked, not as reversing a considered choice.**

**Reachable in production**, which is why this carries a defect marker rather than sitting in Open questions: both routes deployed at run 1415, the feature gate defaults ON when its config row is absent, and the capabilities are granted to existing store-manager and warehouse roles. It is not waiting behind a switch nobody has flipped.

**Open, deliberately not designed here: whether the policy should turn on whether the item had actually been PACKED when it was wasted.** That is the sharper question — a finished unit binned in its jar and a tray of prep binned before it was ever packed are different events, and a single account-level answer treats them alike. **No field records that today.** It is named so it is not later met as a fresh discovery, and **it must not be built on until it is asked for**: adding a per-event packed flag is a larger change than the setting this rule requires, and the setting is what unblocks the defect above.

**Not settled here: the setting's name, where it lives, its default for a new account, and how the two routes are brought onto it.** This settles what is true. How it is built comes later and must answer to this rule.

## 34. Stock is counted by item and place — nothing else

**Decision.** A stock quantity is keyed on exactly two things: the item, and the location it sits in. There is no third dimension. Stock is never keyed on purpose, department, intended use, kitchen-versus-retail, or any other classification.

**Consequence — an item does not know where it is going.** The same item may be consumed in production, sold on a shelf, listed on a sales channel, or all three. Nothing on the item record determines this. A purchase line names the destination location; the item never implies one. Any code or screen that infers a destination from the kind of item is wrong.

**Consequence — a business that wants two counts of one item creates two locations.** A kitchen and a shopfront at the same street address are two locations. So are two shelves in one room. A location is whatever the business says it is; the system does not verify that locations are physically distinct. This is the supported path and it requires no feature, setting or flag.

**Consequence — this is not configurable.** A per-account switch between two-part and three-part keys would require every stock read, write, transfer, count, report and channel sync to handle both shapes permanently. The two-part key is the only shape. Nothing is withheld from any account by choosing it, because the second-location path is always available.

**Rationale.** Purpose is not a property of goods sitting on a shelf; it is a decision made when the goods are moved or used. Recording it on the stock row freezes a decision that has not been made yet, and creates counts that disagree the moment someone uses a bag from the wrong pile.

## 35. Damage on a delivery is a money question, not a stock question

**Decision.** Damaged units are recorded against the purchase line, and every damaged quantity carries an outcome: REPLACING, CREDITED, or UNRESOLVED. The outcome is chosen by the operator when the damage is recorded. There is no default that resolves itself.

**REPLACING** — the supplier is sending fresh units. The amount owed does not change. The delivery is not complete: the order stays open until the replacements arrive or the outcome is changed.

**CREDITED** — the supplier is not replacing. The amount owed drops by the damaged units' value. The delivery is complete.

**UNRESOLVED** — nothing has been agreed yet. The damaged units' value is held: neither owed nor written off. The order stays open.

**Consequence — no account is forced into one outcome.** A business whose suppliers always replace picks REPLACING every time and it costs one click. A business whose suppliers always credit picks CREDITED. Neither is the product's assumption, and neither is hardcoded. See §0.

**Consequence — a purchase order does not close while goods are owed.** An order with REPLACING or UNRESOLVED damage stays open. An order that closes while units are outstanding is an order nobody chases.

**Consequence — damaged units never enter stock**, under any outcome. This is unchanged from current behaviour and is restated here so it is not read as a question this section reopens.

**Rationale.** What happens to damaged goods is agreed between two businesses, not determined by the goods. A system that assumes one outcome is describing one supplier relationship and calling it a rule.

## 36. Finance — a Tacet module for every tenant

**Decided 2026-09-01.**

### It is not Production-gated

Finance ships to every tenant. Every business has money coming in and money going out; a pure reseller with no production still buys stock, pays rent, and needs to know whether it made money. Gating Finance on the Production module would leave a reseller with no accounts screen at all.

Production changes exactly one thing: where the cost of a sold item comes from. For a reseller it is the purchase price of the thing. For a maker it is the recipe rollup — materials, labour, overhead, packaging. That difference lives in the cost engine, which is already gated on Production. Finance reads `unit_cost_at_sale`, which by then is a number, and does not know or care which way it was derived.

This is confirmed by how the category treats the same figure. Restaurant software calls it food cost percentage — cost of goods divided by sales — which is the identical formula to retail gross margin with a different cost source. Same screen, different input.

### It is not accounting

Tacet builds an operational money view, not a bookkeeping system. Explicitly out of scope: chart of accounts, double-entry, tax engine, bank reconciliation, jurisdiction-specific compliance. Odoo does build these and ships fiscal localisations for over a hundred countries to do it; that is a product in its own right and Tacet is not going to become one. Every other system in the category — Shopify, Loyverse, Lightspeed — produces an operational report and hands off to the accountant's own software.

The universal spine, and the whole of what Finance computes:

    Revenue − cost of goods = gross profit − operating expenses = net

Only the top two lines are ever automatic. Operating expenses are typed in by a person, in every system that exists. So Finance is one calculated report plus one hand-entry list, and nothing more.

**AMENDED 2026-09-07 — the spine gains a row, and two of its rows are blank. Neither change touches the reasoning above; Finance is still an operational money view and still not accounting.** §55 rules that hand-typed `income_entries` money-in is NOT revenue and takes **its own staircase row below the revenue line, feeding Net** — the spine as drawn here has no such row, and a reader who takes it as the complete set of rows will be missing one. §56 rules that `cost_of_goods` and `gross_profit` stay null and **render blank**, so the middle two lines are not computed today and Net is revenue minus operating expenses. **"Only the top two lines are ever automatic" is unchanged as a statement about which lines COULD be automatic; today only the first of them is.**

### Revenue derives from orders, not from `sales_entries`

**DECIDED: Finance reads revenue from the order record.**

`sales_entries` is not a revenue source and never was a complete one. It is written live only by manual Sales entry and by market POS. Eleme revenue has never reached it at any point. Meituan, mini-app and gzgrocery reached it only through one-time import scripts run by hand against a specific data dump, wired into no route, cron or startup path. Anyone reading the kitchen app's Finance income total as "all sales" is reading a number that structurally omits one channel entirely and is stale for three others.

Worked example, on a day where Roots takes ¥3,500 across six channels — Meituan ¥1,200, Eleme ¥800, mini-app ¥600, gzgrocery ¥300, dine-in ¥400, market POS ¥200:

- Reading `sales_entries`: **¥600**. Four channels missing or frozen. Reaching ¥3,500 means building sync for four channels into a table §22 already has down for retirement.
- Reading the order record: **¥2,900** on day one with no new sync, because those four channels already write orders. The remaining ¥600 is counter and market trade, which is not an order today.

The rejected option is not merely more work; it is work invested in a table scheduled to die. §21 already governs: an order is a sale, there is one record, and reporting reads from it.

**EXTENDED 2026-09-07 — see §55, which restates this as REVENUE IS ORDERS, AND ONLY ORDERS and settles what this subsection left implicit.** Everything above stands. What §55 adds is the other half of the boundary: **hand-typed `income_entries` rows are money in and are NOT revenue**, so "revenue derives from orders" excludes the typed ledger as well as `sales_entries`. §55 also puts the `sales_entries` half of this subsection back in question — see the pointer under *Counter and market sales become orders* below.

### Structure — two screens

The kitchen app presents six tabs: Dashboard, Income, Expenses, Ledger, Invoices, Categories. Income, Expenses and Ledger are three views of one list. Categories is settings. Invoices is Purchasing's job and is already built there. Tacet ships two:

- **Summary** — the staircase above. Filtered by date range, location and channel.
- **Transactions** — one list, both directions, filterable to in or out. The only surface where a person types.

Categories move to Settings. They are a per-account list a business writes in its own words — not a chart of accounts, not a fixed set, not seeded with anyone else's vocabulary.

**Invoices is not moved and not rebuilt.** Tacet Purchasing already reads the same `invoices` table — the supplier scorecard's "Owed now · 当前应付" tile and bill count come from it. The kitchen Finance Invoices tab is a second front door onto rows Purchasing already owns. It is dropped, not migrated.

### §0 consequences, recorded so they are not re-imported

Three things in the kitchen build are Roots-shaped and are rebuilt rather than carried:

- Expense categories are hardcoded Chinese strings. Income categories are worse: they live in each browser's localStorage and are never synced to the server at all, so there is no shared list, only a per-device accident.
- Currency is `¥` throughout.
- Neither ledger table records a location. A one-shop business does not notice; a fifteen-shop business cannot operate.

### Counter and market sales become orders — DECIDED 2026-09-01

A sale rung up at a till or a market stall is an ORDER. It is written to the order record the same way a Meituan, Eleme, mini-app or gzgrocery sale is, with its line items and with `unit_cost_at_sale` recorded per line.

The rejected alternative was a typed-in daily total on the Transactions list — a single figure with no products attached. It is less work and it is the same mistake this section was written to correct. On a ¥3,500 day with ¥400 dine-in and ¥200 at a stall, that ¥600 would reach the revenue line and reach nothing else: no product margin, no cost of goods, no per-item reporting. Finance and Products would then disagree about the same day, for the same reason the kitchen app's income total has been wrong — a second place where sales live.

§21 already governs: an order is a sale, there is one record, and reporting reads from it. A counter sale is a sale.

**Consequence for tenants without a till.** Most will never create one of these. Nothing about this decision requires a tenant to have counter sales, and no screen should imply they must.

**Consequence for `sales_entries`.** With this decided, every one of the six channels writes orders, and the table has no remaining live writer. Its retirement under §22 stage 8 is now unblocked. Retirement itself is NOT scheduled here.

**QUALIFIED 2026-09-07 — "no remaining live writer" must not be quoted as settled, and the retirement is not unblocked on the strength of it.** The DECISION above is untouched: a till or market-stall sale IS an order. What §55 puts back in question is whether the live code does it. **The kitchen POS writes `sales_entries`, a different table from the `retail_orders` the Tacet Summary counts**, and if till-counter takings land there and not in the order record then Tacet's revenue figure is short by that amount today and no screen says so. **§55 holds this open as a survey question that must be settled before any Finance chart ships.** The sentence above states the consequence of the decision; it is not evidence about what the code does, and it was never a measurement.

### `routes/finance.js` is not fixed — it is blocked and left to die — DECIDED 2026-09-01

`routes/finance.js` has no tenant handling anywhere. All seventeen routes use the module-level global database handle; none calls `tdb()`. The count is seventeen router method declarations in `routes/finance.js`, verified 2026-09-01; an earlier reading of thirteen was wrong, and blocking "the thirteen write routes" by count would miss four. A second tenant reaching these routes would read and write Roots' ledger.

This is a defect, not a design question, and the rule for it already exists. It is nonetheless NOT being fixed in place, and the reason is sequencing rather than severity: the file serves the kitchen app, which is being retired, and Tacet's own Finance routes do not exist yet. Correcting seventeen routes in a file scheduled for deletion spends the effort twice and lands new code in something leaving.

**What ships instead.** The write routes are to be blocked at the route layer, using the same middleware pattern already applied to the thirteen kitchen cost-write routes. Reads are to be left alone.

**Status 2026-09-01: unbuilt.** `blockCostWrite` exists in `middleware/block-kitchen-cost-writes.js` and is imported by `routes/ingredients.js`, `routes/purchases.js`, `routes/recipes.js` and `routes/admin.js`. `routes/finance.js` does not import it, and its nine write handlers carry only `requireAuth`, `requirePermission('finance')` and `requireDelete`.

**Why blocking writes is sufficient and reads are not urgent.** The exposure is a second tenant, and §22 already forbids onboarding one before stage 5 completes. So the read half of the leak has no reachable victim today, while the write half is what would corrupt a ledger if the ordering assumption ever failed. The cheap half is done; the expensive half is deleted rather than repaired.

**This is not a precedent for leaving `tdb()` gaps open.** It applies to code with a scheduled death and a live replacement being built. Any route without both of those is fixed, not blocked.

**Tacet's Finance routes are built on `tdb()` from the first commit.** There is no migration step here to forget, because there is nothing to migrate — the correct version is the only version that will ever exist.

### An expense may carry a location, and blank means the whole business — DECIDED 2026-09-01

Revenue and cost of goods already carry a location, because they come from the order record. Operating expenses do not, and today neither ledger table can record one at all.

**The decision: location is an optional field on an expense. Blank means the cost belongs to the business, not to any one place.**

Worked on Roots, one month. Revenue ¥100,000 (Tianhe ¥60,000, Yuexiu ¥40,000), cost of goods ¥40,000 (¥24,000 / ¥16,000). Typed expenses: Tianhe rent ¥8,000 and wages ¥10,000; Yuexiu rent ¥12,000 and wages ¥7,000; an accountant's fee of ¥2,000 belonging to neither.

- Tianhe: ¥36,000 gross profit − ¥18,000 = **¥18,000**
- Yuexiu: ¥24,000 gross profit − ¥19,000 = **¥5,000**
- Business-wide: **−¥2,000**
- ¥18,000 + ¥5,000 − ¥2,000 = **¥21,000**, the unfiltered net.

The three views reconcile. That is the test the rejected options fail.

**Why the alternatives were rejected.**

*No location at all, as today.* Filtering the Summary to Tianhe would show its ¥60,000 revenue against all ¥39,000 of expenses — Yuexiu's rent included — and report a ¥3,000 loss on a shop that made ¥18,000. **A filter that silently returns a wrong answer is worse than no filter**, because nothing on the screen says it failed.

*Location required on every expense.* The accountant's ¥2,000 would have to be forced onto one shop, making that shop ¥2,000 too expensive and the other ¥2,000 too cheap. The form would be demanding a fact that does not exist.

*Apportion shared costs across locations by a rule.* Sixty-forty on revenue gives Tianhe ¥1,200 and Yuexiu ¥800, and every shop then shows a complete-looking profit. Rejected because the rule is an opinion — one business splits by revenue, another by floor area, another by headcount — and the resulting figure cannot be checked against anything. It would mean building a settings screen for a judgement call and then presenting its output as a measurement.

**The per-location figure is called CONTRIBUTION, never profit.** Profit implies business-wide costs have been taken off, and they have not. The filtered view says Contribution and states the amount it excludes; only the unfiltered view says Net. **The word is the guard against a later session building the apportionment option in order to make the label true.**

**A single-location tenant sees none of this.** No location filter, no excluded-costs line, and the last row reads Net. The dimension exists in the data and is invisible in the interface until a second location does.

**Where the column goes, and its shape, are NOT decided here.** This decides that the dimension exists, what blank means, and what the figure is called.

### PO-derived expenses appear in Transactions as one row per purchase order — DECIDED 2026-09-01

Receiving a purchase order writes expense rows automatically, one per expense category on the PO. They are a projection rather than a record: both posters delete every row for a PO and re-insert them on each status change, so flipping a PO back to Requested makes its expense rows cease to exist, and flipping it forward recomputes them.

Roots' PO-0050 is the concrete case: ¥1,257.68 across two rows, ¥602.68 of ingredients and ¥655.00 of packaging.

**The decision: PO-derived expenses DO appear in the Transactions list, collapsed to ONE row per purchase order, not editable there, and linking through to the purchase order in Purchasing.** PO-0050 is one line reading its number and its ¥1,257.68 total, which opens the purchase order rather than an edit form.

**This is a DISPLAY decision and nothing else.** `postPOExpenses()` and its retail twin continue to write one row per category exactly as they do today. Two rows exist in storage; one row is drawn. Nothing about how these rows are computed, written or deleted changes here.

**Why not hide them.** Transactions would then hold only what people typed. On a month with ¥17,000 of typed expenses and this PO, Transactions would show ¥17,000 while Summary showed ¥18,257.68, with nothing on either screen accounting for the difference. Two screens in one module disagreeing about the same month, silently, is the exact fault §36 was written to correct.

**Why not show them as ordinary rows.** They would be uneditable for no visible reason, and they would vanish when somebody in Purchasing flipped a status — money disappearing from a ledger with no explanation on the screen where it disappeared.

**The grouping and the link are what make the behaviour legible.** One row per purchase order rather than one per category, because the purchase order is the thing that happened and the category split is an internal detail. It is not editable here because it is not edited here, and the place it IS edited is one click away on the row itself. **The row explains its own constraint instead of merely enforcing it.**

**The category hint, and what it does at one.** A PO row carries a quiet note that its figure is a sum of N category subtotals — PO-0050's ¥1,257.68 is two, ¥602.68 of ingredients and ¥655.00 of packaging. **At exactly one category the note disappears entirely. It does not read "1 category".** When N is 1 nothing was collapsed, so a note would assert a breakdown that does not exist and send the operator looking for one; a placeholder that looks like information is worse than silence. Everything else on the row is unchanged at one category — the tint, the posted-by mark and the link out all report provenance and editability, which hold regardless of how the PO split.

**The object is called a purchase order.** Matched to what Tacet Purchasing already ships on screen (`16-purchasing.js`, bilingual with 采购单). "Buying order" is the kitchen app's term and dies with it. The row action reads *Open purchase order* rather than *Open order*, because a bare "order" on a Finance screen can be read as a customer order.

### Categories are normalised on write, and the existing rows are corrected once — DECIDED 2026-09-01

`routes/finance.js` never calls `storeCategory`. A manual income or expense entry writes whatever text the browser sent, with no normalisation of any kind. Purchasing normalises earlier in the chain — `storeCategory` is called when a PO line's expense category is saved, so `postPOExpenses()` copies an already-normalised value into `expense_entries` without calling it itself. Finance has no such upstream step and no `category-text` import at all, so its text is never normalised anywhere.

The consequence is a wrong screen, not untidy data. Three rent payments typed by three people can be stored as three categories that differ only by an invisible Kangxi-radical character or by ASCII spacing — ¥8,000, ¥12,000 and ¥6,000. Summary's expense breakdown then draws three lines that read identically and cannot be told apart, where there should be one line of ¥26,000. **The total is right and every line beneath it is wrong**, which is worse than a visibly broken number because nothing on the screen looks wrong.

**The decision, in two parts.**

**1. Finance calls `storeCategory` on every write.** The same function Purchasing already uses, doing the same job: normalise the text, and snap it onto an existing entry in the `categories` table where one matches by spacing and case. Finance stops being the exception.

**2. The existing rows are corrected once.** Normalising on write alone leaves every row already in the ledger carrying its variant, so the breakdown stays wrong for every month already recorded. A one-time pass rewrites the stored category text on the existing rows to its normalised form.

**Why not normalise on read instead.** Grouping by normalised text at query time would fix history and new rows together without touching storage. Rejected on two counts: the stored values stay dirty, so **every future reader has to remember to normalise and one that forgets reintroduces the fault silently**; and the Transactions list would still draw rows the operator cannot distinguish, because it lists rows rather than grouping them.

**The one-time pass rewrites live financial data and is treated as such.** It changes category text only and never touches an amount, a date or a location. It requires a backup taken immediately before it runs, and a dry run whose output is read by a person before anything is written. `scripts/normalise_finance_categories.js` exists from an earlier survey and is the likely starting point rather than a fresh script.

**Income categories are a separate and unsolved problem.** Expense categories at least share the `categories` table with Purchasing and the ingredient picker. Income categories are held in each browser's localStorage and have never been synced to the server at all — `saveFinCats()` pushes only the expense list. Normalising income text therefore makes the stored values consistent but does not produce a shared list, because no shared list exists. **Where income categories live is a Settings question and is NOT decided here.**

### Tacet's Finance begins on 1 August 2026, and the kitchen app's ledger is exported rather than migrated — DECIDED 2026-09-01

**Nothing is deleted. Tacet's Finance counts money from 1 August 2026 forward.** Everything already in `income_entries` and `expense_entries` stays exactly where it is.

**Why a cutover rather than a migration, established by reading the live data.**

`income_entries` holds 26 rows covering June and July 2026, ¥239,841 in total. `retail_orders` holds ¥113,767 for the same two months. The two do not reconcile, and the reason is not error on either side.

Order coverage was still being switched on across those months — gzgrocery runs 22 orders in June against 111 in July, Meituan's Yuexiu store 11 against 129 — so the order record is partial in June and close to complete by late July. Eleme has zero orders in both months, consistent with never having synced then. By August every channel is present: 587 orders, ¥123,454, the first complete month.

**The largest discrepancy turned out not to be a discrepancy at all, and it is the finding that settles this.** Mini App showed ¥152,309 in the ledger against ¥82,738 of wechat orders. Inspecting the three rows: ¥76,105.69 described `6月` and ¥75,790.00 described `7月`, both recorded as arriving in the company bank account, plus one genuine ¥413.30 Alipay transaction. **The two large rows are month-end settlement receipts, not sales.** They were filed under Mini App because the category list offered nothing meaning "platform payout".

**So the two records were never reconcilable, and this is not a data quality problem. They measure different events.** `retail_orders` records sales. The ledger records cash arriving. A migration would have been reconciling a sales log against a bank statement and calling the difference an error.

**The kitchen app's history is exported to a file, because after the kitchen app is retired nothing else reads those rows.** Leaving them in the database and filtering them out of Tacet would make them unreachable — present, but openable by nobody. A spreadsheet of both tables in full, handed to the operator and their accountant, is what makes "still readable" true rather than nominal.

**Expense rows need no cutover treatment of their own** beyond the date filter. They are already in the table Tacet reads and their category values were verified clean by a live dry run on 2026-09-01. **The table is not a closed historical set.** The export on the same day returned 168 rows spanning 8 May to 29 August 2026 — 76 more than the 92 a survey found on 4 August, because Purchasing has gone on posting expense rows throughout. Roughly a month of them post-date the cutover and are correct, current data rather than history. Tacet counting from 1 August picks them up as it should, so nothing is broken by this, but **"the kitchen app's ledger" names a table that is still being written to, not an archive.** Any later reading of this section that treats those rows as closed history will be wrong.

**Two things were seen in the data and are deliberately NOT resolved here.** `wechat_chat` and `pickup` appear as order channels in August, ¥4,043 between them, and are named in no mapping anywhere in the repository. And settlement — money arriving from a platform after the sale it belongs to — has no home in Tacet's model; recording it in Transactions would double-count revenue the order record has already counted. Both are recorded so a later session finds them rather than rediscovering them.

**The export ran on 2026-09-01.** Two CSVs, UTF-8 with BOM, written to `/root/backups/` by `scripts/export_kitchen_ledger.js` and taken off the box. Income: 26 rows, ¥239,841.06, 13 June to 31 July 2026. Expenses: 168 rows, ¥214,876.88, 8 May to 29 August 2026, 25 of them carrying sub-cent values written exactly as stored. The income figures match the live queries this decision was built on, to the cent.

**SUPERSEDED IN PART, 2026-09-02 — the date filter is gone.** Everything above about why the two records do not reconcile, why the ledger is exported rather than migrated, and why nothing is deleted STANDS. What does not stand is **“Tacet’s Finance counts money from 1 August 2026 forward”** and the **“date filter”** the expense paragraph leans on: there is no such filter and there is to be none. See *Finance is not floored at the cutover date* immediately below. A reader who meets this section first should read its cutover as answered there.

### Finance is not floored at the cutover date — DECIDED 2026-09-02

**Finance reads `expense_entries` and `income_entries` for whatever periods they cover. There is no 1 August 2026 floor on either screen or on the transaction form.**

§36’s earlier cutover reasoning was about cost of goods and stands: `unit_cost_at_sale` capture begins 31 August 2026, measured, so **gross profit does not exist before then and both cost lines read Not recorded for earlier periods.**

**That reasoning does not extend to expenses.** Production holds **111 expense rows across May, June and July totalling ¥180,332.28.** They are real, they are complete, and there is no cost dependency in them. **A screen that hides ¥180,000 of recorded spending to keep one line uniform is less true than one that shows the spending and marks the missing line as missing.**

**This supersedes the form’s date min of 2026-08-01, decided earlier the same day.**

**Both cost rows keep reading Not recorded UNCONDITIONALLY and take no date condition.** v4.113 decided that a missing staircase step is shown and marked, never hidden and never zero, and lifting the floor does not qualify it. Making the rows conditional on the period would replace one rule a reader can hold with two that disagree at a boundary — and **the cost reader is not built, so there is nothing for such a condition to switch between.**

**SUPERSEDED IN PART, 2026-09-07 — the rows are BLANK, and UNCONDITIONALLY is exactly why this is a one-token change. See §56.** The rule this paragraph exists to defend is untouched and is the reason §56 could be written in one line: **one rule a reader can hold, no date condition, no boundary at which two rules disagree.** §56 keeps all of that and changes only what the two cells contain — blank rather than Not recorded. **The cost reader is still not built**, so as above there remains nothing for a condition to switch between; §56 states when that changes, which is when §31 lands and the two rows fill from it and nothing else.

**A FINDING RECORDED WITH THE DECISION: THE FLOOR WAS NEVER IN THE CODE.** A survey on 2026-09-02, taken before anything below was written, found the literal `2026-08-01` in no file under `routes/`, `lib/`, `public/`, `reference/` or `docs/` — only in `scripts/`, as a window bound and as fixture dates in test seeds, neither of which is a floor. (It appears in `routes/` and `public/` today only inside comments that exist to say there is no floor, and the two Finance suites read comment-stripped source so those sentences cannot satisfy the assertion they describe.) `resolveWindow` in `lib/finance-window.js` is the whole of Finance’s date logic and clamps nothing; both endpoints filter on the resolved window alone; the range bar’s Today/7/30/90 presets are unclamped, so 90 days already reached back past the cutover; and **`#fin-tx-date` has never carried a `min`.** The floor existed in three comments and nowhere else — `routes/finance-transactions.js` and `public/retail-admin/22-finance.js` asserting it as a live constraint, and `scripts/export_kitchen_ledger.js` resting on it for its own justification. **All three are corrected, and the absence is now asserted rather than merely true**, in the markup and in the two Finance suites, because an untested absence is one confident reader away from being filled in.

**`scripts/export_kitchen_ledger.js` STAYS, with its premise corrected.** Its header said the pre-cutover rows would be **“reachable by nothing once the kitchen app is retired”**; that is now false, since Transactions reads them. The export is not withdrawn by that, because unreachability was never its only reason: **a CSV in the accountant’s hands needs no login, no tenant and no running server, and it is a snapshot of the tables as they stood — which a live screen, by construction, is not.**

**One consequence, so it is not read as a defect.** `income_entries` runs 13 June to 31 July 2026 and holds nothing after it. **The money-in list is therefore empty in any window starting in August or later, the default trailing 30 days among them, and fills with those 26 rows when the range is widened back.** That is the ordinary §1.12 empty state either way, not the seventh state, and v4.118’s reading of it is unchanged — only its stated cause is, which was the cutover and is now simply the last row’s date.

**Two rows those 26 include, flagged rather than filtered.** *Tacet’s Finance begins on 1 August 2026* records that ¥76,105.69 (`6月`) and ¥75,790.00 (`7月`) are **month-end settlement receipts filed as Mini App income**, and §36’s *Settlement receipts are excluded from Finance entirely* gives settlement no row in Transactions. Widening the range now DRAWS them, because they are rows in `income_entries` and this screen lists that table. **They are not filtered out**: no column distinguishes a settlement receipt from any other income row, so a filter would have to match on description text and would silently drop real income that happened to be described the same way — §36’s own refusal, "a filter that silently returns a wrong answer is worse than no filter". **They do not double-count revenue**, because Transactions is a list and not a summand: the Summary’s top line reads `retail_orders` and never this table. **Where settlement belongs in the model remains open**, as §36 already records.

### Settlement receipts are excluded from Finance entirely — DECIDED 2026-09-01

**Revenue comes from the order record. A settlement receipt has no representation in Finance: no place in the staircase, no row in Transactions, and no income category.**

A sale is counted at the moment the order exists. A platform payout is that same money arriving in the bank — the same yuan, later, by a different route. Recording a payout as income therefore does not add a second sale; it counts one sale twice.

**This closes "Where settlement receipts belong", the open item §36 has carried since v4.108.** That bullet is left standing in *Explicitly NOT decided here* below rather than struck out, on the convention that superseded text is not edited. This subsection supersedes it: a reader who meets the bullet first should read it as answered here.

**Four consequences, recorded because each is a thing a later session might otherwise build.**

**1. Transactions keeps exactly two directions.** Money in and money out. No third "payout" type is added to hold settlement, and no direction is added for anything else on the strength of this decision.

**2. No income category means, or is permitted to imply, "platform payout."** The absence of such a category is what caused the Mini App mis-filing in the first place — the operator had money arriving from a platform and a category list with nowhere to put it, so it went under the channel it came from. **The fix is not to add the category.** Adding it would take a mistake that happened twice and make it easy, repeatable and correctly labelled, which is worse than leaving the operator with nowhere to file a thing that does not belong in this ledger at all.

**3. The ¥152,309 filed under Mini App is confirmed, and its shape is now known.** It is two hand-totalled summaries of daily platform arrivals — ¥76,105.69 described `6月` and ¥75,790.00 described `7月` — plus one genuine ¥413.30 sale. **They are not monthly transfers and they are not sales.** The month names describe the period each summary covers, not a single month-end movement of money, which is what "month-end settlement receipts" above was read to mean before the daily cadence below was established. **Only the ¥413.30 is revenue.**

**4. Settlement receipts belong to settlement reconciliation, attached to the channel connection.** That is where a bank arrival is checked against what the orders said the channel owed. It is not the Finance staircase, and nothing about this decision puts it there.

**COLLISION RECORDED 2026-09-07, NOT RESOLVED — §55 puts `income_entries` ON the staircase, and two settlement receipts are sitting in that table.** §55 gives hand-typed `income_entries` money-in **its own staircase row below the revenue line, feeding Net**. This subsection says settlement has **no place in the staircase**. On the live data those two rulings meet: consequence 3 above establishes that ¥76,105.69 (`6月`) and ¥75,790.00 (`7月`) are settlement summaries filed as Mini App income, **¥151,895.69 of the 26 rows in `income_entries`**, and *Finance is not floored at the cutover date* establishes that **no column distinguishes a settlement receipt from any other income row** — which is why those rows are drawn rather than filtered on the Transactions list, a filter having to match on description text and being refused for it. **A money-in staircase row summing that table would therefore carry ¥151,895.69 of settlement into Net, which is the double-count this subsection was written to prevent.** Transactions could hold the rows harmlessly because it is a list and not a summand; a staircase row is a summand, and the reasoning that made drawing them safe does not carry over.

**This is NOT decided here and is NOT decided by §55, which does not reach it.** Neither ruling is bent to fit the other: §55 stands as written and this subsection stands as written. **What is owed is a ruling from Ash on which of three things happens** — the two rows are corrected at source so the ledger stops holding settlement as income, or the money-in row excludes settlement by some means that is not a description-text match, or §55's row is scoped to something narrower than the whole table. **It is recorded here, against the ruling it collides with, so that whoever builds the money-in row meets it before writing the sum rather than after.**

### Meituan settles daily, not monthly — DECIDED 2026-09-01

**A correction to the working assumption carried through the Finance design sessions.** Meituan pays into the company bank account per day, not as a month-end lump.

This does not change what Finance counts — the decision above already excludes settlement from Finance entirely. It changes the shape of the settlement reconciliation work already queued on §36:

- **The comparison is per channel per day, not per channel per month.**
- **For each day:** sum `channel_settle_amount` across that day's orders for the channel, and compare it against the amount that arrived in the bank.
- **A mismatch localises to one day's orders rather than a month's**, which is the practical argument for the daily cadence rather than merely a consequence of it. A month-shaped check tells the operator that something is wrong somewhere in several hundred orders; a day-shaped one hands them the orders to look at.
- **`channel_settle_amount` is 预计 — a forecast, revised on refund, not a bank confirmation.** The daily check therefore compares a forecast against an actual arrival, which is not a like-for-like comparison and is not meant to be. **Small divergences are expected, and they are the signal the check exists to surface. They are not by themselves errors.**

**Eleme's settlement semantics remain unresolved, and this cadence is recorded for Meituan specifically.** The two channels do not even store the field the same way: Meituan's writer takes the latest poll (`channel_settle_amount = COALESCE(?, channel_settle_amount)`, `routes/meituan-internal.js`), while Eleme's keeps the first value it ever saw (`COALESCE(channel_settle_amount, ?)`, `routes/eleme-internal.js`). A forecast that is revised and a forecast that is frozen do not support the same check. **Do not extend the daily cadence to another channel on the strength of this entry.**

**Nothing is scheduled, designed or built here.** Settlement reconciliation remains unbuilt work. This records its cadence and the comparison it makes, not its delivery.

### `wechat_chat` and `pickup` are mapped, and the open item asking what they are rested on a wrong premise — DECIDED 2026-09-01

**Closes "What `wechat_chat` and `pickup` are", the open item §36 has carried since v4.108.** That bullet is left standing in *Explicitly NOT decided here* below rather than struck out, on the convention that superseded text is not edited. This subsection supersedes it: a reader who meets the bullet first should read it as answered here.

**They are not platform channels and they were never unmapped.** They are staff-keyed order ORIGINS — how the customer reached the shop — written by the New order form's "Order came from · 订单来源" dropdown, alongside `wholesale` and `other`. All four are `MANUAL_ORDER_ORIGINS` in `routes/retail.js`, and `source` already records that a person keyed the row.
